summary: Kent C. Dodds frames his talk around the vision of every person having a Jarvis-like AI assistant, using an Iron Man movie clip to illustrate capabilities such as database compilation, on-demand UI generation, accessing public records, cross-dataset joins, flight plan creation, and doorbell answering. He argues most capabilities are technologically feasible today except holographic displays, and the real barrier is integrations—no single company will build integrations for every possible service, especially niche ones. He traces three phases of AI assistant evolution: Phase 1 began with ChatGPT, which answered questions but required manual copy-paste of context; the host application layer made it pivotal. Phase 2 saw host applications adding integrations like search engines and calendars, but these were limited by developer availability and proprietary plugin systems. Phase 3 is MCP, a standard protocol all major AI assistants support or will soon support. Service providers build MCP servers exposing tools, resources, prompts, and sampling. The host application creates standard clients, dynamically manages services, and tells the LLM what is available so it can select appropriate tools. Dodds then demonstrates MCP in Claude Desktop with three servers: Locationator for device location, a weather server, and EpicMe for journaling with OAuth 2.1 authentication. The demo shows the LLM chaining tool calls—getting location, checking weather, authenticating via email token, creating a journal entry with auto-generated tags, and retrieving and formatting the entry as markdown. He notes users must currently approve every tool call, unlike Tony Stark's trust model with Jarvis, but expects this to improve. He highlights that MCP servers can be accessible only via MCP rather than as web applications, representing a shift from browser-based interaction to natural language AI interaction where users simply state what they want to accomplish and the AI performs the task. He closes with resources including the MCP specification and his platform epicai.pro.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Jarvis Vision
sections.summary: Kent C. Dodds introduces himself and his course platform epicai.pro, then shows an Iron Man clip where Jarvis compiles databases, generates UIs, accesses public records, performs cross-dataset joins, shows related news, creates a flight plan, and answers the doorbell. He notes most of these capabilities are technologically feasible today, except holographic displays.

sections.title: The Integration Problem
sections.summary: Dodds explains the barrier to personal Jarvis assistants is integrations. No company will build integrations for every possible service, especially niche ones like local government pavilion reservations. Without a standard mechanism, it is not worth wiring up partial integrations. MCP provides this standard mechanism for AI assistants to communicate with arbitrary tools and services.

sections.title: Three Phases of AI Assistant Evolution
sections.summary: Phase 1: ChatGPT (~3 years ago) answered questions but required manual context management. The host application layer, not the LLM, made it pivotal. Phase 2: Host apps added integrations (search, calendar, Slack) but were limited by developer time and proprietary systems. Users want one Jarvis, not multiple wrappers. Phase 3: MCP enables universal tool access via a standard protocol supported by all major assistants.

sections.title: MCP Architecture Details
sections.summary: The host application communicates with the LLM and dynamically manages available services. It creates standard clients for each service. Service providers build MCP servers that expose tools, resources, prompts, and sampling. The LLM knows what is available and selects the most appropriate tool. Service providers retain control of their integrations.

sections.title: Live MCP Demo in Claude Desktop
sections.summary: Dodds demonstrates MCP in Claude Desktop with three configured servers: Locationator for device location, a weather server, and EpicMe for journaling. The demo chains tool calls: getting current location in London, checking weather, authenticating via email with an OAuth 2.1 token, creating a journal entry with auto-generated tags, and retrieving the entry formatted as markdown. He notes users must approve each tool call currently, unlike Tony Stark's trust model with Jarvis. MCP servers have authentication built in via OAuth 2.1. The LLM intelligently formats JSON responses as readable markdown.

sections.title: Future of Interaction and Closing
sections.summary: Dodds highlights that the EpicMe MCP server is accessible only via MCP, not as a web application, representing a shift from browser-based to natural language AI interaction. Users no longer need to learn special search query formats; they simply state their goals and the AI performs the task. He shares resources including the MCP specification and his platform epicai.pro with workshops, cohorts, and posts about AI's future in user interaction.
